label: Exercises for Act II
notes: This review session spans printed pages 83 through 93 and consolidates the metric chapters of Act II. We restate the first fundamental form, conformal maps, the pseudosphere, and hyperbolic isometries, then work representative problems by building a model, measuring an invariant, and checking what survives a change of coordinates.

label: The First Fundamental Form
notes: Every surface measurement starts from the metric. We recall how the first fundamental form encodes lengths, angles, and areas through three coefficient functions, and we stress that these coefficients are intrinsic data: they let an inhabitant of the surface do all geometry without ever leaving it or seeing the ambient embedding.

label: Worked Problem A: Sphere Metric
notes: Our first worked exercise parameterizes the round sphere and reads off its metric from the speed of coordinate curves. We compute the coefficients directly, confirm that meridians and parallels meet at right angles, and note the shrinking parallels that make the metric vary with latitude rather than being flat.

label: Conformal Maps
notes: A conformal map preserves angles by scaling the metric by a single positive factor. We restate this condition, explain why the off-diagonal coefficient must vanish and the diagonal ones must agree, and emphasize that conformality is exactly the statement that infinitesimal circles map to infinitesimal circles, never to ellipses.

label: Worked Problem B: Stereographic Projection
notes: Stereographic projection is the canonical conformal chart of the sphere. We sketch the projection from the north pole, derive its conformal factor as a function of distance from the origin, and verify the angle-preserving property by watching the coordinate grid stay orthogonal everywhere in the plane image.

label: The Pseudosphere
notes: The pseudosphere is the tractrix surface of revolution, the constant negative curvature counterpart of the sphere. We recall its profile curve, write its metric in the strip coordinates that reveal hyperbolic structure, and stress that it realizes a piece of the hyperbolic plane as a genuine surface sitting in ordinary space.

label: Worked Problem C: Curvature of the Pseudosphere
notes: Here we confirm that the pseudosphere has constant curvature minus one. Using the half-plane form of its metric we apply the curvature formula for a conformally flat metric, carry out the logarithmic derivatives, and obtain a clean negative constant, matching the saddle-like geometry visible in the surface.

label: Two Models of the Hyperbolic Plane
notes: Hyperbolic geometry has two standard pictures: the upper half-plane and the Poincare disc. We restate both metrics, identify their geodesics as vertical lines and circular arcs meeting the boundary at right angles, and prepare to move objects between the two models using a single conformal transformation.

label: Hyperbolic Isometries
notes: The isometries of the hyperbolic plane are exactly the Mobius transformations that preserve the boundary. We restate the Mobius form, recall that these maps act conformally and send geodesics to geodesics, and classify them as elliptic, parabolic, or hyperbolic according to their fixed-point behavior on the boundary circle or line.

label: Worked Problem D: A Mobius Geodesic Transfer
notes: We carry a half-plane geodesic into the disc with the Cayley transform. Tracking three boundary points through the map, we show that a vertical line becomes a diameter and a semicircle becomes a boundary-orthogonal arc, confirming that the transformation is an isometry between the two hyperbolic models.

label: Lorentz and Spacetime Metrics
notes: Act II closes with the indefinite metric of spacetime. We restate the Minkowski line element with its crucial sign flip, contrast its light-cone structure with the positive-definite surface metrics, and note that hyperbolic geometry reappears as the geometry of the unit timelike hyperboloid of constant proper time.

label: Recap and Invariants
notes: We close by collecting the invariants that survived every exercise: lengths and angles from the first fundamental form, the conformal factor that scales without distorting angles, constant negative curvature on hyperbolic models, and isometry classes under Mobius maps. The lab habit is to construct, measure, compare with a theorem, then perturb.
